Concentration and oscillatory limits

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A distributional limit records what remains after averaging against a smooth test. A narrow positive kernel can leave a point mass. A rapidly oscillating smooth function can disappear, while a corner or a logarithm leaves a nonzero contribution. Two parameters can select different limits, and a family converging away from one point can still fail to converge on the whole space.

All pairings are complex-linear. Unless another space is specified, convergence means convergence against every . Our Fourier convention is The full proofs of rapid Fourier decrease, the inverse identity and the Gaussian mass are in the supplied Fourier foundations, F2–F4. Order, positivity and distributional limits, Section 1, supplies the test topology. We use Cauchy kernels and distributional boundary limits, Theorem 4.1, for the existing pole boundary distribution; Finite parts of singular powers, Proposition 5.1, for ; and the general even-function argument in Odd powers and collapsing hyperbolas, Lemma 2.1, for smooth square-variable descent. Their exact uses appear below.

The supplied scalar calculus, §§12–13, proves compactness, cutoffs and the fundamental theorem of calculus. The supplied integration foundations, §§15.0–15.4, 15.6 and 16, prove convergence, smooth approximation, Fubini and planar sector areas. The polar integral formula needed below follows from those areas by uniform approximation in the proof of Theorem 6.

Here is the polar integral formula for the continuous compactly supported integrand at hand. Partition into radial and angular intervals. Their images partition the disk, except for finitely many rays and circles of area zero. Formula (PC5) in §15.6 of the integration foundation gives the area of each annular sector as the integral of over its parameter rectangle. Choose one sample point per rectangle. The sums of its sampled integrand times these areas are therefore identical in the two coordinates. The image diameter of a rectangle is at most , by the fundamental theorem for sine and cosine. Uniform continuity on the disk makes both approximation errors at most times a modulus of continuity tending to zero with the mesh. This applies to complex integrands using absolute errors, and proves equality of the two integrals. The origin and the repeated angular endpoint have area zero and contribute nothing.

When a distributional limit is locally uniform

Theorem 8 (uniform gradient control). Let be open and . Suppose that for every compact there is with If in , then is represented by a locally Lipschitz function and converge to it uniformly on every compact subset of .

Proof. Fix a closed ball , and let be its common gradient bound. The fundamental theorem along segments gives This holds for complex values as well, using the Euclidean norm of the complex gradient and the ordinary Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

We prove uniform Cauchy convergence on . Given , choose so small that ; using in the denominator makes such a choice also valid when . A finite -net covers this compact ball. For each center choose a nonnegative smooth test , supported in , with integral one. These supports lie inside .

Whenever , every in the support of satisfies . From (L35), For each of the finitely many tests, the integrals converge by the given distributional convergence. They are therefore simultaneously Cauchy: for all large , their differences have absolute value less than . Two applications of (L36) give . Completeness of the complex numbers defines a pointwise limit, and this same uniform Cauchy bound proves uniform convergence to it. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous; passing to the limit in (L35) makes it -Lipschitz on the smaller ball.

Every compact subset of has a finite cover by such smaller balls. The local limits agree on overlaps, since they are limits of the same pointwise sequence. Thus they define a locally Lipschitz function on , with uniform convergence on each compact. For every test , uniform convergence on its support gives . The original distributional convergence gives the same limit , so as distributions.

Compact profiles and their surviving moments

A complex profile can have zero mass while retaining a higher moment. The integral Taylor formula supplies the exact multivariable remainder used here; no positivity or symmetry of the profile is assumed.

Taylor's integral formula gives the degree- polynomial, with remainder Since , integrating its absolute value proves (M3). The polynomial integrates to . Use and divide by . All lower coefficients vanish, and the error is at most times the displayed derivative seminorm. Bounded subsets of have that seminorm uniformly bounded; bounded compact-test families do as well, by U008, (T1)–(T2). Its degree- derivatives isolate this coefficient, and the limiting pairing is . The converse is immediate.

A boundary preserves an oscillatory jet

On the whole line, Lemma 1 gives Thus every fixed power disappears on compact tests. Cutting the oscillation at one endpoint changes the conclusion.

Theorem 10 (one-sided endpoint expansion). Fix , and , and set For every integer and every compact smooth test, Consequently strongly in . In distribution notation the -th term of the expansion is .

Proof. Write for and . Integration by parts gives The endpoint at infinity is zero by compact support. In particular its sign at zero is retained. Iterate (M10) times and multiply by . The first terms are those in (M9); the remaining two are and . Their absolute values give the asserted bound. On a bounded compact-test family, the integral norm is bounded by the length of one common support interval times a derivative supremum. Taking proves strong convergence. Distributional differentiation supplies the stated coefficient signs.

The jump, rather than rapid oscillation alone, accounts for the point mass. In particular the positive and negative frequency signs give opposite imaginary masses.
